title: Death as a work of nature
hook: death is like teething, growing up, having children: one of nature's works (Meditations 9.3)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was pulled thread: one small wrong puckers the whole cloth. Your line was we're one fabric.

A baby is cutting teeth: fussy, drooling, awake at three in the morning. Nobody calls it a tragedy. It's hard, it hurts, and everyone in the house knows it's just what babies do on the way to growing up. Marcus picks up exactly that ordinary picture and sets it beside something we usually treat very differently. It's a tender subject, so gently: today we read his thought on dying.
screen: `A BABY CUTTING TEETH.` → `HARD, BUT NATURAL.` → `DEATH AS A WORK OF NATURE.`

segments.voice: In book nine Marcus writes: don't despise death, but be content with it, since it's one of the things nature wills. Then he names the others. Being young and growing old. Growing up and reaching full size. Getting teeth, a beard, gray hair. Conceiving, carrying a child, giving birth. All the works our seasons of life bring. Dying, he says, belongs on the same list. He doesn't say rush toward it, and he doesn't say ignore it. He says wait for it the way you'd wait for a child to be born: not anxious, not careless, knowing it comes in its own time. That, he says, is how a thoughtful person meets it. Then a homelier consolation, the kind that reaches the heart: think of the things you'll leave, and the habits of the people you'll no longer have to live among. But in the same breath he checks himself. Don't be offended with them, he writes. Care for them, and bear with them gently. This is a Stoic view, and not everyone holds it. Many traditions speak of death in terms of a soul, a judgment, a world to come, or rebirth, and Marcus himself, across the book, is unsure what follows. What he offers here isn't a teaching about the afterlife. It's a posture: to see dying as part of the same nature that brought teeth and gray hair, and so not to meet it with horror.
screen: `TEETH, GRAY HAIR, BIRTH, DEATH.` · `WAIT AS FOR A BIRTH.` · `A HOMELIER COMFORT, CHECKED.` · `A POSTURE, NOT A DOCTRINE.` · then, large: `NATURE'S WORK.`

segments.voice: This one is gentle. If the subject is tender for you right now, simply rest with the breath; that's enough. Otherwise, bring to mind the changes your body has already lived through, first teeth, a growth spurt, a first gray hair, maybe a pregnancy or a child, each on its own schedule, and let one quiet thought sit beside them: my life has a shape, and an ending is part of the shape.
Cutting teeth. Marcus sets dying beside this, and growing old, and gray hair: just one more of nature's works, waited for, not dreaded. Today's word.
Your line: nature's work. On Marcus's view, as ordinary as teeth and gray hair. Go gently.

howItsDone: Stoic readers often reflect briefly on mortality as part of nature's ordinary course, alongside growing up and growing old, as a way of meeting it calmly rather than with dread.

chat.says: What did Marcus mean, comparing dying to a baby cutting teeth?
options: He saw dying as one of nature's works, like growing old, to be met calmly, not with horror.
He meant we should never speak or think about it at all until it arrives.
He meant we can always tell when it's coming, the way teething shows its signs.
chat.meaning: In 9.3 Marcus lists dying with growing up, teeth and gray hair: works of nature, waited for calmly. Other traditions see death differently.

Marcus.meaning: Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor who wrote the Meditations

Stoic.meaning: the Greek and Roman philosophy Marcus followed

consolation.meaning: words that comfort someone facing loss

notes: 9.3 paraphrased: do not despise death but be content with it as one of the things nature wills (youth, age, growth, teeth, beard, gray hairs, begetting, pregnancy, birth); wait for it as for the child to come from the womb; the 'common' (Long: 'vulgar') comfort that reaches the heart: the objects you leave and the manners of those you no longer live among; yet do not be offended with them but care for them and bear with them gently.
